title: NAFTA and the Local Labor Market
research_question: Did the tariff reductions implemented under the North American Free Trade Agreement reduce wage growth for U.S. workers, and were these effects concentrated among particular industries, geographic localities, and educational groups? Specifically, did workers in industries and locations more exposed to Mexican import competition experience disproportionately lower wage growth, including spillovers to non-tradable service-sector workers in vulnerable areas?
data_description: The study uses 5% samples from the U.S. Census for 1990 and 2000, drawn from IPUMS at the Minnesota Population Center, covering workers aged 25-64 with positive prior-year income (about 10.3 million observations). Worker-level variables include age, gender, marital status, race, English-speaking, educational attainment (less than high school, high school, some college, college graduate), industry of employment (89 traded-goods industries), Consistent Public-Use Microdata Area (conspuma) of residence, and pretax wage and salary income. U.S. tariffs on Mexican imports at the 8-digit HS level come from Romalis/Feenstra-Romalis-Schott data, concorded to Census industries. Mexico's revealed comparative advantage is constructed from U.N. Comtrade bilateral trade flows. Additional data include Trade Adjustment Assistance petitions (1994-2000) and Chinese import shares by industry. The unit of observation is the individual worker, with industry- and conspuma-level tariff measures merged in.
institutional_context: NAFTA, signed in 1993 by the U.S., Canada, and Mexico, scheduled a gradual phase-out of tariffs on Mexican imports beginning in 1994 and continuing for ten years (with some extending to fifteen). The negotiated liberalization schedule varied substantially across sectors: some industries faced rapid tariff elimination during 1990-2000, while others retained much of their initial protection beyond 2000. Initial tariff levels also varied widely across the 89 traded-goods industries, ranging from zero to 17%, with footwear, apparel, canned fruits and vegetables, and textiles among the most heavily protected. Because U.S.-Canada tariffs had already been eliminated under the prior Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement, the relevant policy variation concerns Mexico. Localities differed in their exposure depending on the mix of industries employing local workers, generating geographic heterogeneity in vulnerability—politically salient in places like Youngstown, Ohio, that attributed economic decline to the agreement.
